import math, random, itertools
rng=random.Random(7)

labels_b=[1,2,2]
def mean(x,s,labels):
 out=[0.0]*3
 for j in range(3):
  i=(j-1)%3
  e=labels[i] if s[i] else 0
  h=0.0 if e==0 else (x[i]-x[j] if e==1 else -x[i]-x[j])
  out[j]=2*x[j]+math.cos(x[j]+h)
 return out
err=0.0
for _ in range(1000):
 x=[rng.uniform(-3,3) for _ in range(3)]
 for s in itertools.product([0,1],repeat=3):
  err=max(err,max(abs(a-b) for a,b in zip(mean(x,s,labels_a),mean(x,s,labels_b))))
print('Maximum conditional-mean discrepancy over 8,000 configurations:',err)
print('Single permutation of nonzero labels exists:',any(all(p[a-1]==b for a,b in zip(labels_a,labels_b)) for p in itertools.permutations([1,2])))

strengths: Conditional summary graphs provide a useful representation of changing interactions. Under the source-state factorization, representing K graphs instead of K^N global regimes offers a meaningful contribution, and the extension of amortized causal discovery is well motivated.

SDCI combines shared interaction functions, graph neural networks, and latent-state inference into a coherent framework. Distinguishing observed, observation-dependent, and recurrent states helps clarify the modeling problem.

The empirical results are promising: fixed-structure particle experiments show excellent recovery, and the determined-state GRN model improves F1 to 0.347 versus 0.187 for the strongest reported baseline. NBA experiments provide additional evidence of predictive usefulness.

The appendices provide substantial architecture, optimization, and data-generation details. The paper also acknowledges unresolved estimator consistency and the practical difficulty of recurrent-state inference.
weaknesses: Theorem 4.3's edge-label identifiability has a counterexample under the stated assumptions. Consider scalar messages f1(a,b)=a-b and f2(a,b)=-a-b, with f0=0 and the permutation-invariant aggregator g(b,{h})=2b+cos(b+sum(h)). With one active incoming edge, either nonzero type produces 2b+cos(a), although their source derivatives are distinct and the aggregator derivatives are nonzero almost everywhere. On a three-node directed cycle with each source switching its outgoing edge on/off, assignments (1,1,2) and (1,2,2) therefore give identical conditional distributions but cannot be aligned by one global label permutation. Corollary A.8 incorrectly treats permutation invariance as implying equal aggregation derivatives across nodes and states. Stronger restrictions are needed for this central guarantee.

The regime-identifiability proof also needs additional justification. In Theorem A.6, Equation (35) applies Gaussian-mixture identifiability at a fixed observation history to identify every regime and their number. For genuinely deterministic states, only one component is active at that history. The assumptions do not supply the support or reachability conditions needed to identify all components and match them across observation regions. Consequently, the claimed coverage of determined states and unknown K does not follow from the presented argument.

The exact-inference claim in Section 3.3 and Appendix B.2 is not justified for the implemented finite-temperature softmax states. Future observations generally inform the posterior over a state, so equating the full state posterior with its local generative distribution is not exact. Shared source states also couple outgoing messages, and nonlinear aggregation prevents the elementwise marginalization asserted around Equation (56). The implementation may remain useful as a variational approximation, but its inference and complexity claims need correction.

The empirical comparisons need stronger calibration and uncertainty reporting. In Table 1, SDCI and Rhino have almost identical AUROC (0.936 versus 0.933), despite very different F1 scores; threshold selection and precision-recall results are therefore important. Training-seed counts, error-bar definitions, and permutation alignment for label/state scores are not adequately specified. Most particle comparisons evaluate summary graphs against stationary baselines, while the regime-aware R-PCMCI comparison uses predefined settings after difficulties with short sequences. These choices limit conclusions about superiority in state-dependent graph recovery.

The application evidence supports a narrower scope than some claims suggest. GRN evaluation uses one simulated bifurcating network and longitudinal measurements of individual cells that Appendix C.2 acknowledges are unavailable in standard sequencing experiments. NBA forecasting has no causal ground truth, and improvements over ACD are modest; it demonstrates predictive utility without validating the inferred causal edges. These empirical merits do not resolve the central theoretical and inference issues driving my weak-reject assessment.
